Yes, a dynamic sized hash table is hard to prove unless you just take it axiomatically. How are you demonstrating that Insert(“Alice”, True) followed by Insert(“John”, True) does not result in memory stores that cause Get(“Alice”) to not return True? Or result in Get(“Blorg”) giving a different value? How are you proving that you can lift this generically so you can reason about non-interference considering only the abstract interface? So you can generically reason that Insert(x, _) allows you to continue to assume that Get(y) is unchanged if x != y even in the presence of dynamic resizing and copying of the underlying data in a hash table implementation? How are you proving that about the keys the leaf piece of code does not even know about? How are you proving that no other operation violates that abstract data model and can thus be ignored for the purposes of your proof? And as a corollary, how do your proofs start failing if a violating operation is added? Sure, if you just assume you have a magical key-value map that does not interact with the concrete data model, then life is easy because you skipped the hard part. Being able to easily encapsulate a data model into a higher-abstraction data model is the thing that is largely missing. It is why formal proofs generally stop in the low hundreds of lines proving a single data structure and its operations. Building and proving you implement usable abstractions that can be reasoned about by your proof system at the abstract level is extremely hard with current systems.

PeerJS does wrong by forcing opening data channels for you, it's already forcing you into a specific opinion on how it should work. Also, it doesn't work in Node.js. I understand their API idea but it should have been one level lower first, to build on top. like-webrtc gives you the RTCPeerConnection perfectly negotiated, connected, cross-platform (browsers, Node, React Native), etc but nothing else then you can open a data channel the way you want. Imagine a TCP or HTTP server/client API, this is the same but you get a peer connection with no extra assumptions and it's up to you what you do next. WebRTC in servers is also important, e.g. imagine long-running bots or literally just run your backend using WebRTC lol. - TCP (congested) + HTTPS (insecure centralized global CA) + JSON (slow) versus - UDP (low latency) + RPC (request/response) + binary encoding (fast) We should start running our centralized backends with WebRTC as a first step to adopt and improve tooling around WebRTC. That's why I compiled and released a modern WebRTC build version for Node.js: https://github.com/LuKks/webrtc-runtime (no signaling, no features, etc) That allows you to use RTCPeerConnection cross-platform anywhere, so I used webrtc-runtime to build like-webrtc (complete solution).

K15 – Turn a static site into a 14 KB bootable x86-64 HTTPS OS

What just served 15kb.org is a 2-vCPU Hetzner VM booting straight into a 14,245-byte x86-64 binary, with the site's files packed directly behind it in the same disk image. There is no Linux kernel, libc, filesystem, shell, or SSH daemon underneath. One NASM file implements boot -> long mode -> virtio-net -> ARP/IPv4/TCP -> TLS 1.3 -> HTTP/1.1. Source and benchmarks: https://github.com/FileSherlock/k15 One command packs a directory of static files (plus pre-compressed .br and .gz variants, ETags, and certificates) into a bootable image you can run in QEMU or write onto a standard Linux cloud VM's disk alongside GRUB: ./k15 pack site/ -n example.org -i 203.0.113.7 ./k15 run build-example.org ./k15 deploy 203.0.113.7 build-example.org A few implementation details and trade-offs that came out of building it: - 128 bytes of RAM per held TLS connection, regardless of file size. Sent TLS records are never buffered in memory. Each segment is sealed on the fly (up to 45 TLS records per virtio TSO frame), and if TCP drops a segment, k15 recomputes and re-seals that exact record from the read-only image and sequence number. Half-open SYNs cost 0 bytes via SYN cookies. - Handshake speed comes from everything around the crypto, not the crypto itself. On the same 2-vCPU VM, k15 does 7,500–9,000 full TLS 1.3 handshakes/s (~2x nginx + BoringSSL, ~4x nginx + OpenSSL) and 105k–125k keep-alive requests/s. OpenSSL's X25519 and P-256 assembly are actually ~20% faster than k15's; k15 takes ~460k cycles per connection vs. 1.0M–1.9M because there are no syscalls, sockets, allocators, or X.509 parsers in the path. - Nothing to break into. Page tables enforce W^X (code and packed site are read-only; packet buffers and stack are NX), the crypto has no secret-dependent branches or table lookups, it never initiates outbound connections, and the IDT is empty. Any CPU fault triple-faults and resets the machine. - TCP without SACK bites on lossy links. Doubling the congestion window up to 367 KB made high-RTT transfers fast on clean paths, then lost 91 segments at once on an emulated 20 Mbit/s bottleneck and took 23.6s to recover one hole per RTT. Without SACK, k15 now grows the window by 1 MSS per 64 KiB ACKed past 64 KB, and caps at 64 KB if a connection sees loss. - Why SSL Labs gives 15kb.org an A (zero warnings) instead of A+. I initially assumed missing post-quantum key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) caused the cap, until checking letsencrypt.org, which gets A+ without PQC on the same grading version. SSL Labs' 2009q criteria require TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV for A+, which cannot be tested against a server that only speaks TLS 1.3 (older versions get a protocol_version alert). - Clunky on purpose. Updating content or renewing Let's Encrypt means building a new image locally and rebooting for a few seconds (`./k15 renew` generates the P-256 key locally so only a CSR touches temporary Linux before rebooting back into k15). IPv4 + virtio-net only, GET/HEAD only, TLS 1.3 only, one site per VM. Full methodology and caveats for the nginx/BoringSSL/OpenSSL/Caddy numbers: https://github.com/FileSherlock/k15/blob/main/bench/README.m...

Hey HN! I'm Lakshay. Raveen and I have built Cerulion, a ROS2-compatible robotics runtime written in Rust. We've worked hard on lowering IPC transport latencies without making the single process tradeoff or forcing POD message types. These fast multi-process graphs can then be resimmed deterministically, and existing ROS2 nodes/launch files can run unmodified alongside native Cerulion Rust/Python code. Installation and quickstart (with a one-shot prompt for your favorite coding agent) here at the repo README: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion I worked on off-road autonomy during my PhD at MIT, and we kept running into inter-process latency in ROS (2 lidars and 6 cameras). Loaned messages need POD types, which nukes standard, vendor-agnostic Image/PointCloud2. We ended up running some hot paths in a brittle single process, which made debugging a nightmare. I'm sure you've seen the heisenbugs ROS-based stacks can produce, with no way to easily reproduce the consumption order or interleaving of callbacks. Valuable data of runtime failures on the robot was hard to use effectively without deterministic reproducibility. This is what we fix. Cerulion bags record per-input reads and scheduler traces alongside message content in standard MCAPs. bag play --resim all --verify re-executes node code on the recorded schedule and compares each byte for exact matches or within defined tolerances. Exit 0 is a match, 1 shows the first topic/frame that diverges, 6 shows schedule divergence and --report gives an optional CI verdict. Eligible ROS2 processes can replay deterministically as well. Here's the data loop: 1. Run: Dependency-ordered level-based DAG scheduler with periodic/data/sync triggers, I/O deadlines, backpressure, and automatic profiling for process partitioning. Each node by default free-runs in its own process while preserving deterministic replay. Live runs pause/resume, and UMWAIT/WFE parks idle consumers on CPUs that support it. Wall-clock reads and runtime thread spawns in user code rejected at compile time by macros. ROS 2 is supported with rmw_cerulion for Foxy, Humble, Jazzy and Lyrical, that lets you run ROS2 nodes/launch files unmodified in the same graph as native Cerulion nodes. LD_PRELOAD gives ROS2 code shared memory loans through std::vector/std::string. cerulion ros2 attach folds in already-running ROS2 robots, and cerulion ros2 run/launch lets you run existing ROS2 workspaces on Cerulion without any additional setup (with an optional automatic migrate suggested that rewrites C++ publish sites). 2. Move: iceoryx2 shared memory with no serialization, no payload copy and no payload-sized allocation, including for variable-length messages like sensor_msgs/Image and PointCloud2. Round trip latency for a 1MiB sensor_msgs/Image between two processes is 4.08µs p50, with a tight tail of 7.38µs p99 (under 2x p50), with recording on . This is default Cerulion, against 10.95 ms for default ROS 2 Jazzy. Cerulion's p50 and p99 stay flat from 64B to 16 MiB. 3. Capture: With this round-trip latency, there are no tradeoffs, not for process isolation and not for bagging. We can afford always-on or event-based logging. Flashback is our robot dashcam: keeps ~30s of all logs and message contents in memory and saves it automatically on process crashes, topic stalls or declared incidents/manual triggers. 4. Reach: A free account lets you pair robots and desks, letting all your devices find each other with no config, IP addresses or discovery chatter. Pubsub is authenticated and on-demand, with signed grants that the robot verifies offline. We use Iroh to hole-punch or relay over WAN, and mDNS over LAN to transmit data using QUIC. Remote topics mirror into local shared memory, and each device has a single network gateway. 5. Diagnose: cerulion doctor scans for compile/run-time issues (better than Windows Troubleshooter I promise) and suggests fixes. Hindsight is an early access MCP to let agents analyze your bags. To get started: go to the repo, install Cerulion with the curl one-liner, and paste the prompt in Claude Code/Codex: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion#quickstart-run-reco... . Or shift your own gears, it's all in the repo that you should star! The CLI needs a free account, which we use to make device pairing as easy as AirDrop USED to be ;) Everything runs on Linux (x86_64/ARM64), macOS and Android (JNI), with more platforms coming. We'd love to hear your feedback! If you run ROS 2 on a real robot, point this at your stack and tell us what breaks. Docs: https://docs.cerulion.com Site: https://cerulion.com

Ginux is a much narrower research prototype. o It is not just namespaces or seccomp policy: those mechanisms partition or filter host-kernel behavior. Ginux additionally supplies contract-specific results and virtual kernel objects such as process identities, /proc, /sys, devices, and lifecycle state. o It is not VM-equivalent isolation: there is no guest kernel or hardware-enforced guest boundary, and current trusted host surface is substantial." https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/main/docs/how-ginux-... >"The problem Ginux explores Linux maintains a broad, stable userspace ABI because general-purpose software depends on it. That commitment is essential for Linux, but a particular workload often needs much less authority. Ginux asks whether an operator can describe that smaller interface as one portable, reviewable instance recipe: o which syscalls and ioctls may execute; o which filesystem paths, devices, sockets, and resources are visible; o which operations are read-only, writable, virtualized, mediated, or denied; o what /proc, /sys, process identities, machine identity, and lifecycle the workload observes; and o which named workload and tests establish compatibility with that contract. This is deliberate ABI reduction, not accidental Linux incompatibility. Ginux does not promise that an arbitrary Linux program will run." Ginux looks absolutely awesome! (Also, it should be pointed out that even though Ginux does not promise that an arbitrary Linux program will run, probably 99% of them will with the correct settings, and 100% of them probably could, with the appropriate source code changes / recompile). What Ginux (and similarly niched Linux userspace proxy / userspace API proxy tools like gVisor) promise is that if your Linux program does run under it, you'll have one heck of a lot more control over what it can do and what it can't do and tracking what it does do, than Linux alone -- which is especially important for AI Agent sandboxing. Will it be the last tool in this category? Probably not! But it (and similar tools in this niche, like gVisor) are well worth watching!

I have started learning Lean this year and have recently stumbled on the concept of subtypes in Lean: For a subtype S of a type T, an element is a tuple <t, P t> of an element t of type T and a proof of a predicate P on t. An example of this could be the subtype AuthenticatedUser of the type User or the subtype SearchTree of the type BinaryTree. Any time you want to change the element (By updating user data or by inserting a node in a tree), you have to reattach a proof for the modified element or the type-checker will straight up reject it. It is, of course, a lot of work to (re)construct the proofs, but for me this strikes the perfect middleground between "formalize all your code and try to finish before retirement/bankruptcy" and "just ship and hope you didn't mess up". If you have a critical part of your software, you can formalize some characteristic on it and guarantee (!) that no one further down the pipeline will mess it up. And you can do that while leaving most of your other code untouched.

The big clue that'll jump out to any rust dev is the type signature: pub const fn toggle(&mut self) The "&mut" says that toggle takes a mutable reference to the instance it is called off of. This is also called a mutable borrow. You might think that would get buried in the program because you don't always check the type signature of every method you call, but there are a few reasons that muts really jump out in rust. The languages immutable by default nature is one and the other is that several IDE have features to specifically draw attention to mutable instances/references. It's a fairly common pattern in rust to have helper methods on a type that take a mutable reference or ownership of self. TL;DR: Rust's ownership model is very unique. Once it clicks its the cat's pajamas, but experience in other languages don't map well to this part of the language.

We made a dsl for this that has routing, classification, code nodes, etc to build these workflows.
